title: gpu-oom-debug-notes-nora-alvarez
content:
Context / short summary:
- Intermittent CUDA OOMs on model-serving node (g4dn.xlarge-ish, 16GB). Failures started after a recent base image update (ubuntu + cuda 11.7). Happens ~1-2x/day, usually under bursty traffic; sometimes after a deployment.
- Symptoms: RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory and occasional driver/runtime mismatch logs in container start.

Commands I ran / quick checks:
- nvidia-smi -L && nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -> GPU shows 0: Tesla T4, 15109 MiB total. memory.used spikes to ~12GB when the OOM occurs.
- docker ps && docker inspect <container> | grep -i gpus -A2 || true -> container launched with --gpus all via nvidia-container-runtime.
- nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o TDPL & (checked processes) -> found some stray jupyter/sidecar processes occasionally. Killed them.
- ps aux | grep python && lsof /dev/nvidia* -> confirmed only our worker processes are attached during failures.
- curl localhost:9090/metrics | grep gpu_memory   (our exporter) -> memory usage climbs over time on affected hosts.
- docker logs <container> (tail) -> shows: RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 2.00 GiB (GPU 0; 15.11 GiB total capacity; 13.70 GiB already allocated; 1.41 GiB free; 2.01 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)
- dmesg | tail -n 50 -> occasionally: NVRM: Xid (PCIe Bus Error) 31 or GPU reset messages around same time as OOM (unclear cause).
- Check CUDA / driver mismatch:
  - inside container: python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda); print(torch.cuda.is_available()); import ctypes; print(ctypes.CDLL('libcuda.so.1'))" -> torch.version.cuda == '11.7', torch.cuda.is_available() == True, but ctypes load sometimes throws: OSError: libcuda.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory (intermittent).
- ldd $(python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda._CUDA_HOME + '/lib64/libcudart.so')") || true -> pointed out missing symlink to installed driver libs in some images.
- dpkg -l | grep -i nvidia; ls /usr/local/cuda-*/lib64 | head -n 10 -> base image has CUDA toolkit 11.7 libraries but host drivers are from 470.x (older) on a couple hosts.
- journalctl -u nvidia-persistenced -n 200 --no-pager -> found nvidia-persistenced died on one host after kernel update; restarted it.

Observed error snippets (copied from logs):
- "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 2.00 GiB (GPU 0; 15.11 GiB total capacity; 13.70 GiB already allocated; 1.41 GiB free; 2.01 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)"
- "OSError: libcuda.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory" (on container start, rare)
- "CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version" (one host after kernel/driver skew)
- "CUDA kernel errors might be asynchronously reported at some other API call" in backtrace (suggesting earlier failure)

Hypotheses / root-cause candidates:
1) Model / batch / traffic combination exceeds available memory transiently (most likely). Sequence length and batch size spikes cause momentary OOMs.
2) Memory fragmentation due to long-running process + varying request sizes + caching (KV cache not being freed, attention caches building up).
3) Driver <-> runtime mismatch on a subset of hosts (we saw >=1 host with older driver -> intermittent libcuda not found or runtime mismatch). Containers rely on host driver; if mismatch, symbol loading or resets can cause crashes that look like OOM.
4) Stray processes / memory hogs on host occasionally occupying GPU memory (sidecars, debug notebooks).
5) PyTorch caching/reservation behavior: reserved bytes cause less free memory; allocation fails because reserved not freed by caching heuristics.
6) Kernel/firmware GPU errors (Xid 31) leading to GPU reset and then OOM on restart.

Mitigations / fixes I tried (and results):
- Reduced per-request batch size from 8 -> 4 and seq_len cap -> 1024. Result: incidence drop (~80% reduction) but not eliminated. Suggests workload spikes are contributor.
- Enabled torch.cuda.empty_cache() at end of each request handler and garbage collection (gc.collect()). Result: small improvement but not full fix (expected, only helps fragmentation).
- Turned on AMP (autocast + GradScaler) for some workloads -> reduced memory footprint by ~30% where applicable. Not universally usable for all endpoints.
- Restarted nvidia-persistenced + docker restart on suspicious hosts -> eliminated intermittent libcuda load OSError for that host.
- Replaced base image on one instance that had missing symlinks; verified libcuda visible inside container.
- Upgraded NVIDIA driver on one host from 470.x -> 530.x (matching CUDA runtime in container). Result: no further "driver insufficient" logs on that host; still sees occasional OOMs under load.
- Set environment var TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 on a couple nodes (to help fragmentation as per PyTorch docs). Result: modest improvement in allocation success rate.
- Added a pre-start check in our entrypoint to fail fast if libcuda is missing (exit 1 and re-schedule) to avoid noisy/useless restarts.

Repro steps (minimal):
- Use our base image (redwood/worker:cuda11.7-2026-01) on a T4. Run simple load test: 16 concurrent requests of long-generation tasks (seq_len 2048, beam 4) for 10 minutes. Watch nvidia-smi.
- Reproduce faster in interactive: python script that allocates large tensors in loop until OOM (see test_oom.py below).

test_oom.py (quick):
import torch
for i in range(1000):
    try:
        a = torch.randn((1024,1024,6), device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)  # tune dims
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print('OOM at iter', i, e)
        break

(This mimics allocation pattern, not exact model pattern.)

Next steps / TODOs (actionable):
- Short term (next 48h):
  - Keep reduced batch sizes / seq_len caps on heavy endpoints (config flag).
  - Add autoscaler rule to prevent > N concurrent heavy-gen requests on same machine.
  - Add startup entrypoint check for libcuda & driver version and emit clear metric.
- Medium term (1-2 weeks):
  - Standardize host driver to >= CUDA runtime version used in images (coordinated driver upgrades across fleet). Create playbook for rolling driver upgrades with health checks.
  - Improve monitoring: per-container libcuda presence, driver vs runtime mismatch metric, nvidia-smi exported per-pod, and Xid error alerts.
  - Experiment with TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF defaults and max_split_size_mb tuning across workload types, measure tail latency + OOM frequency.
  - Investigate memory fragmentation further: instrument allocation patterns (torch.cuda.memory_snapshot() on failure) and keep traces for analysis.
- Long term (quart):
  - Consider fallback to lower-memory model variant or model sharding for very bursty workloads.
  - Explore pre-warming / process isolation: run heavy requests on dedicated pools or use a sidecar that schedules allocation more safely.

Notes / miscellaneous:
- Found a host where kernel had been updated without driver rebuild -> produced libcuda load errors intermittently. Fix was full driver reinstall + reboot.
- Potential race between container runtime starting and nvidia-persistenced; adding a small wait/retry in entrypoint helped.
- Keep an eye on Xid errors; those often indicate hardware/driver instability, not just app-level OOM.

Quick references / commands to reproduce checks: (copy/paste)
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv
- docker run --gpus all --rm -it redwood/worker:cuda11.7-2026-01 bash -c "python -c 'import torch; print(torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())'"
- python -c "import ctypes; ctypes.CDLL('libcuda.so.1')"  # quick check for driver visibility
- TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 python -c "..."

If anyone else is hitting this on a particular pod/container, pls paste:
- output of nvidia-smi (full) at failure time
- `docker inspect` for the container
- container logs around the exception
- host kernel + driver: uname -a; cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version

Handy links (internal):
- Confluence: confluence.redwood/display/ENG/GPU+OOM+playbook (draft)
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime -> pinned notes (see linked artifacts)

-- Nora
